## What I created

- SubsetJuliaVM (a.k.a `sjulia`)
  - Supports a subset of Julia's syntax
  - A stack-based VM (Virtual Machine) implemented in Rust
- Runs on iOS and Android devices
  - The VM compiles to WebAssembly, so it also runs in the browser
- Supports parts of Plots.jl, OrdinaryDiffEq.jl, AbstractAlgebra.jl, and more

## Deliverables {.smaller}

**iOS / iPadOS** — a native app with no JIT, fully App Store compliant

### Google it `SubsetJuliaVM`

## Why I created it {.smaller}

- I wanted to run Julia on my iPad
- But Julia normally relies on **JIT** compilation — and iOS blocks JIT twice:
  - **The OS blocks it** — W^X: memory is writable **xor** executable
    - A JIT *writes* machine code, then *executes* it
    - → it needs pages it can write **and** then execute
    - **General-purpose JIT is unavailable to ordinary distributed apps** —
      Apple reserves it for its own apps like Safari's JS engine
      (exceptions: approved browser engines, debugger-attached dev builds) —
      [Apple Platform Security](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/security-of-runtime-process-sec15bfe098e/web)
  - **The store forbids it**
    - Apps may not download, install, or execute code that introduces or changes
      app functionality —
      [App Store Review Guidelines §2.5.2](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#2.5.2)
- A **bundled interpreter** is fine: bytecode is just *data* read by an
  already-signed app (downloaded code would still fall under §2.5.2)

## What about Binder or Google Colab?
  - Unusable where the internet connection is unreliable
  - Installing external packages takes a long time

## How I created it

- Apps like Pythonista and Carnets do run on iOS.
  - So why not build a virtual machine that accepts Julia syntax?!
- I don't have an ability to create this
  - Let's use AI
  - Built with heavy use of AI tools: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, DeepSeek, Kimi, etc.

## Let's actually build it!
  - A stack-based bytecode interpreter (**no JIT**)

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"useMaxWidth": false, "nodeSpacing": 25, "rankSpacing": 32, "padding": 10}}}%%
flowchart LR
  SRC["Julia source"] -- parse --> CST["CST"] -- lower --> IR["Core IR"] -- compile --> BC["bytecode"] -- "stack VM interprets" --> OUT["result"]
```

Result: [AtelierArith/julia-vm-oss](https://github.com/AtelierArith/julia-vm-oss)

## How sjulia differs from upstream Julia {.smaller}

How code is interpreted and executed:

Each cell: *who does it* → *what it produces*

| Stage | Upstream Julia | SubsetJuliaVM |
|------|-----------|---------------|
| Parsing | flisp / JuliaSyntax.jl → AST | pure-Rust parser → CST |
| Lowering | Julia's lowering → lowered IR | Rust lowering → Core IR |
| Code generation | LLVM **JIT at runtime** → native code | bytecode compiler **before execution** → bytecode |
| Execution | CPU runs native code | stack VM interprets bytecode |
| Runtime library | C runtime + pure-Julia `base/` | Rust builtins + a pure-Julia subset |

- With no JIT, SubsetJuliaVM **runs even on iOS (W^X) and WASM**

## What SubsetJuliaVM does *not* provide {.smaller}

Everything that would break the sandboxed, offline, no-downloaded-code model:

- **Pkg.jl / package management** — no `Pkg.add`, no registry, no downloads;
  `using X` only reaches the ~34 packages bundled into the binary
- **Network I/O** — no Sockets, no Downloads/HTTP
- **Filesystem access** — file operations are unimplemented;
  `include` resolves through virtual embedded paths
- **External processes** — no `run(cmd)`
- **C interface** — no `@ccall`/`pointer`/`unsafe_*`
- **Real parallelism** — single-threaded by design;
  Tasks/Channels are cooperative continuations
- **Native-code reflection** — no `@code_llvm`/`@code_native` (there is no LLVM);
  use `sjulia --dump-bytecode` instead

More details: see the [Appendix slides](appendix.html)

## Mandelbrot heatmap

```{=html}
<div class="sjulia-executor" data-code="using Plots\nfunction kernel(c, n)\n  z = 0.0+0.0im\n  for k in 1:n\n    abs2(z) > 4 && return k\n    z = z^2 + c\n  end; n\nend\nxs = range(-2, 1; length=80)\nys = range(\n  -1.2, 1.2;length=60\n)\ncs = xs' .+ im .* ys\nzs = kernel.(cs, Ref(40))\nheatmap(xs, ys, zs)"></div>
```

## Lorenz attractor (OrdinaryDiffEq)

```{=html}
<div class="sjulia-executor" data-code="using OrdinaryDiffEq\nfunction lorenz!(du, u, p, t)\n    du[1] = 10.0 * (u[2] - u[1])\n    du[2] = u[1] * (28.0 - u[3]) - u[2]\n    du[3] = u[1] * u[2] - (8 / 3) * u[3]\nend\nu0 = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]\ntspan = (0.0, 60.0)\nprob = ODEProblem(lorenz!, u0, tspan)\nsol = solve(prob, Tsit5(), dt=0.05, saveat=0.05)\nusing Plots\nplot(sol, idxs=(1, 2, 3), title=&quot;Lorenz attractor&quot;)"></div>
```

## `juliars`

![](assets/julia-vm-oss.png){.absolute top="80" right="0" width="170"}

- A Julia-to-Rust transpiler (experimental)
- Unlike JuliaC, it does not require `libjulia`

```sh
$ cargo build --release -p subset_julia_vm \
```

## Performance: Julia vs. SubsetJuliaVM {.smaller}

Mandelbrot set benchmark (Apple Silicon macOS, measured 2026-07):

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```julia
function mandel_point(c::ComplexF64,
                      maxiter::Int64)::Int64
    z = 0.0 + 0.0im
    for k in 1:maxiter
        abs2(z) > 4.0 && return k - 1
        z = z * z + c
    end
    return maxiter
end

function mandel_count(width, height, maxiter)
    total = 0
    for y in 1:height
        ci = -1.2 + 2.4 * (y - 1) / (height - 1)
        for x in 1:width
            cr = -2.0 + 3.0 * (x - 1) / (width - 1)
            total += mandel_point(cr + ci * im, maxiter)
        end
    end
    total
end

mandel_count(1500, 1500, 500)  # same source for all implementations
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
| Runtime | Time |
|-----------|-----:|
| Upstream Julia | 0.50 s |
| `juliars` (AoT) | 0.52 s |
| sjulia **VM** | 4.0 s |
| Python 3.14 | 20.8 s |

- AoT is **about as fast as upstream Julia**
:::
:::
